summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, request logs, and error analysis for Atlas Health. Focus on how to locate failed requests, investigate model fallback behavior, parse request metadata (customer id, model version, route), and run ad-hoc debugging with raw request logs. Discussed hosted vs Dedicated tradeoffs, VPC/private deployment considerations, and security controls (SOC2, KMS, SSO). Next steps: send security docs, run benchmark with sample payloads, schedule pilot kickoff.
transcript:
15:00:02 Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm ava from Redwood, with diego and nia from our se team. we got about 50 minutes, we'll walk through the console tracing and request logs and then leave time for q and a. 
15:00:18 Priya (Atlas CTO): Thanks, ava. quick context: we're evaluating inference infra for our clinical summarization pipeline. P95 latency target is around 300ms for most requests, some longer batch jobs ok. security and auditability are big for us. 
15:00:32 Ava: got it. diego, do you want to take first pass on the tracing demo? 
15:00:36 Diego (Redwood SE): yeah, i'll share my screen. so this is the Redwood Console tracing tab, top-level you get a timeline of requests, by default it shows last 24 hours, you can filter by model, route, customer id, status code, and by latency buckets. the trace view groups spans for request routing, kv cache hit/miss, compilation stage, and model inference. 
15:00:55 Marcus (SRE): quick question — how definitive are the KV cache hit annotations? last provider we used showed 'cache hit' but it was just an approximation. 
15:01:05 Diego: good point. for us the KV cache hit flag comes from the serving runtime and is tied to the request id propagated through the runtime. it's accurate for prefix cache hits and we also log the cache key fingerprint. there are edge cases for near-duplicate prefixes but you can see the raw request log to confirm. 
15:01:22 Hannah (ML Eng): can you show a failed request flow — like when model fallback happens? we saw some hallucination cases and want to trace back. 
15:01:31 Diego: yeah, absolutely. i'll filter to status != 200, should be some errors and fallbacks. here is a request where our smart routing fell back from a low-latency quantized variant to a higher-precision model due to capacity. you can see the route decision span, the reason 'capacity limit' and the fallback span with model version. 
15:01:50 Priya: sorry, did you say 'quantized variant'? is that something we need to manage? we worry about quality regressions when switching variants. 
15:02:01 Diego: not at all — the platform exposes quality profiles per variant in the catalog. plus you can pin a route to a model version to avoid automatic fallback. there are also rollout policies for canary and A/B. we'll show the rollout config after the trace. 
15:02:18 Sam (Security): how long are request logs retained by default? and are they encrypted at rest? 
15:02:26 Ava: default retention for hosted is 30 days for request logs, longer retention available as an add-on or with Dedicated/Private. all logs are encrypted at rest with customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. we'll attach the KMS integration notes in the follow-up. 
15:02:40 Marcus: if we go Dedicated, can we keep logs in our VPC? 
15:02:44 Ava: yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and private log sinks. Private on-prem supports fully customer-controlled storage. 
15:02:51 Diego: back to the trace — if you click the request id you get the full request timeline and the raw request payload, which is scrubbed for pii by default but you can configure scrubbing rules. here you can see token timings, per-kernel latency, and the model's top-level error if present. 
15:03:12 Hannah: the raw payload looks a bit chopped in the transcript view — is that a transcription thing or console truncation? 
15:03:18 Diego: console truncates in the UI for long payloads but you can download the full raw request as a .json. the transcript here — sorry, the auto transcriber sometimes makes 'k v cache' into 'kay vee cache' in our transcripts, so ignore the weird text. 
15:03:33 Priya: we need to be able to search by correlation id from our app logs, is that possible? 
15:03:38 Diego: yes, we encourage instrumenting a customer_request_id header; that gets indexed and you can search or pivot from that id straight into the trace and raw logs. 
15:03:48 Ava: quick note — request logs include model_version, route, redwood_customer_id, and SSO user if present. for compliance you can map team ownership to audit logs. 
15:04:00 Marcus: show us an error that required debugging — something like a 503 or a model time out. 
15:04:06 Diego: filtering to timeouts now. here's a request with a model timeout: trace shows compilation span stalling and then a timeout error code at the runtime layer. the error analysis panel suggests probable causes — large sequence length, an unexpected tokenization mismatch, or kernel OOM. it also links to matching past failures so you can see if this is recurring. 
15:04:27 Hannah: tokenization mismatch — can we compare the tokenizer used at serving time to the training one? 
15:04:33 Diego: yes, the model metadata includes tokenizer version and checksum; we surface that in the trace metadata and in the model catalog entry. you can also view sample inputs that triggered mis-tokenization. 
15:04:45 Priya: are these logs SAML-friendly — like can we control who sees raw payloads? 
15:04:50 Ava: yes, RBAC controls whether a user can view raw request payloads. for Private/Dedicated you can limit raw payload visibility to security and SRE roles via SSO groups. 
15:04:59 Sam: and this integrates with our existing SAML provider? 
15:05:04 Ava: we support SAML/SSO and OIDC; we will include a short SSO integration guide in the follow-up. 
15:05:11 Diego: moving on, here's the error analysis view — it aggregates error types by route and model version, shows trends (errors per hour) and highlights regressions after rollouts. for example, after a simulated canary we had a spike in 'invalid input' errors which you can drill into and tie to a specific prompt change. 
15:05:33 Marcus: question — can we alert on those regressions? 
15:05:36 Diego: yes, you can create alerts based on error rates, latency SLO breaches, and model quality regressions tied to eval sets. alerts can route to pagerduty, slack, or a webhook. 
15:05:47 Hannah: the eval integration — does it automatically run after rollouts? 
15:05:51 Diego: you can configure automatic eval runs post-rollout; Redwood Optimize can run your test prompts and surface quality deltas. for the pilot we'd recommend an eval set focused on clinical summarization edge cases. 
15:06:05 Priya: in our environment we have PHI concerns — default scrubbing is okay but we might need stricter controls. how do you handle redact rules? 
15:06:14 Ava: scrubbing rules can be customer-defined regexes and we support removing or hashing PII before logs are stored. in Private setup logs can be stored on your side and never leave your network. we'll include the redact example rules. 
15:06:28 Diego: small demo of a debugging flow: we got an alert, open the trace, pivot to raw logs, download the payload, replay request in a sandbox using the same model_version and env — you can reproduce locally with the replay tool. reproduction often surfaces tokenizer or prompt formatting issues. 
15:06:49 Marcus: how do you manage replay creds — we don't want to expose production secrets to replay. 
15:06:54 Nia (Redwood SE): replay tooling supports obfuscated secrets and token replacement; we provide a safe replay token that limits scope to the sandboxed environment and respects role permissions. 
15:07:05 Priya: for performance, our critical path needs sub-300ms P95. how do you guarantee latency? 
15:07:11 Diego: for hosted we have latency SLA tiers and automatic routing to low-latency pools; for strict P95 we'd suggest Dedicated where you get reserved capacity and predictable tail behavior. we can also tune batching and KV cache policies per workload. 
15:07:26 Hannah: can you show the per-kernel timing breakdown? that was mentioned. 
15:07:30 Diego: yes, in the trace span breakdown you can see pre-processing, compilation, attention kernels, and post-processing — each has timing. here you can see a kernel taking most of the time which suggested we recompile with a different kernel or change sequence length limits. 
15:07:46 Priya: kernel selection — is that automatic? 
15:07:49 Diego: runtime does automatic kernel selection based on model arch and observed seq length distribution; for Dedicated we can also lock in a kernel profile if you want reproducibility. 
15:07:58 Marcus: about data residency — if we keep logs in our region, is the console still functional? 
15:08:04 Ava: yes, Private can run a local console or a secure tunnel to a cluster in your region. UI experience is same, metadata is surfaced through the control plane but logs stay in region per your compliance needs. 
15:08:16 Priya: okay sounds good. let's talk pricing briefly — the baseline hosted vs Dedicated commit. 
15:08:21 Ava: high level: hosted is per-token and per-embedding usage, Dedicated is committed monthly GPU capacity with discounts and predictable throughput. we'll share a pricing spreadsheet with projected costs for your current traffic patterns. 
15:08:31 Marcus: final Q — how do you correlate request logs with billing? we need to make sure high-cost routes are visible. 
15:08:37 Ava: the Console and cost explorer show token-level cost per route and model version; you can see per-request cost and aggregate by route. 
15:08:46 Priya: cool, that's useful. 
15:08:50 Diego: quick recap: how to debug — 1) find alert or correlation id, 2) open trace, check spans for runtime/kernel/kv cache, 3) download raw payload, 4) replay in sandbox, 5) if it's capacity-related consider pinning model or requesting Dedicated. 
15:09:06 Ava: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the SOC2, KMS, SSO notes and schedule the benchmark. any final questions? 
15:09:15 Sam: none from security for now, thanks. 
15:09:18 Priya: thanks, ava and team. we'll coordinate on sample logs. 
15:09:22 Ava: great, talk soon! 
15:09:25 [call ends]
